description_full: JBS N.V., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the processing of animal proteins, encompassing activities related to beef, pork, lamb, and poultry worldwide. The company is involved in the production and marketing of prepared foods and other related products, as well as operations in leather, collagen, hygiene and beauty products, metal packaging, biodiesel, and other related businesses. It offers its products under the Seara, Doriana, Pilgrim's, Moy Park, Primo, Friboi, Maturatta, Swift, Ozo, Adaptable Meals, and other brand names. The company was founded in 1953 and is based in Amstelveen, the Netherlands.

financial_summary: JBS N.V. is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $13.3B market cap on $86.2B of annual revenue.

Returns on capital run at 14% against a 9% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 13% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $833M in free cash flow — roughly 1 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.31× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.6× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and thin 2.0× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 11.9% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 58% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Payout ratio of 143% leaves essentially no coverage if earnings wobble

Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 12% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.78, it is more defensive than the market.
About $75.8M trades a day, enough to build a position, and interest is running hot at 1.5x its yearly average volume.
val: The stock trades 53% below its DCF fair value of $26.56, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 3%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $5.90 to $75.61 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: EV/EBITDA 7.5 vs 10.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.4% (vs the 8% bar).
The 15 covering analysts target $18.18 on average, 47% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 5.2% annual cash-flow growth, 7pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 14% earns above the cost of capital of 8.5%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar.
It runs a 13% gross margin and converts 1% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.31x.
ROE of 26% is amplified by 5.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.6x net debt to EBITDA ($4.6B of cash against $21.1B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, and interest cover is thin at 2.0x.
growth: Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has missed earnings estimates by 5.1% on average.
Analysts expect 53.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 57.7%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 34%.
It returns 11.9% a year to shareholders (8.1% in dividends).
It pays out 143% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 17.3% of the float, 5.4 days to cover.
people: With about 283,000 employees, each generates about $305K of revenue, 0.6x the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $3K of free cash flow per employee.
